standard.title: Select and combine elements of music
standard.description: select and combine elements of music when composing and practising music for performance
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have created arts works that communicate ideas (AC9AMUFC01) and made deliberate choices during making. They have explored voice, body percussion and sound sources through play (AC9AMUFD01). They have no formal vocabulary for elements of music and have not yet deliberately selected or combined musical elements.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students select and combine elements of music when composing and practising music, using at least two elements deliberately to create expressive or communicative effects.

nodes.label: What elements of music are
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can name and demonstrate at least three elements of music (e.g. tempo, dynamics, pitch, rhythm) and identify them when listening.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three named elements of music in a piece of music heard; demonstrate each by making a sound or movement that represents it.
nodes.typical_width: Name and demonstrate elements including tempo (fast/slow), dynamics (loud/soft), pitch (high/low), duration (long/short), and identify them in a range of musical examples (songs, chants, instrumental music).
wider: Listen to contrasting pieces and identify which elements change and which stay the same — e.g. 'The tempo slowed down but the dynamics stayed loud'
Explore elements through body percussion — create sounds that demonstrate fast/slow, loud/soft, high/low using only body and voice
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot name and identify elements of music as distinct variables, they cannot make deliberate selections. All subsequent composing and practising decisions in this standard depend on students having a shared vocabulary for elements. Without it, directions like 'vary the tempo here' or 'what element could you change?' are inaccessible.

response_modes.reason: Build element vocabulary through naming + demonstrating + listening in combination. Games like echo clapping (rhythm), call-and-response pitch matching, and move-with-the-beat activities build the aural recognition that makes vocabulary meaningful rather than just memorised labels.

success_criteria: Can name at least three elements of music when prompted
Can identify each named element when listening to a musical example (e.g. points to the fast/slow change)

nodes.label: Combining elements to create effects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can combine two or more elements of music deliberately to create a specific expressive effect (e.g. fast and loud to create excitement, slow and soft to create calm).
nodes.minimum_width: Combine two elements of music (e.g. tempo + dynamics) to create a composition or section with a described effect.
nodes.typical_width: Combine multiple elements across different composition types — e.g. combining pitch and rhythm in a melody, combining dynamics and articulation in a song performance, using contrasting sections (fast/loud then slow/quiet) to create expressive structure; improvise with voices and body percussion.
wider: Create a composition with at least two clearly contrasting sections (e.g. sound/silence, fast/slow) and describe the expressive effect of each
Improvise a melody with a drone accompaniment — experiment with combining pitch patterns and decide which combinations sound best together
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to combine elements deliberately — not just vary one at a time — is the composing move this standard requires. Without it, students' compositions are single-element variations rather than multi-element creations. This cascades to AC9AMU4C01 which requires manipulating elements (plural) to communicate ideas.

response_modes.reason: Combination decisions are easier to make when students have encountered many examples of how combinations create different effects. Listening to contrasting pieces and analysing which elements are combined helps students build a mental library of effect-combination relationships.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The space of possible element combinations is genuinely rich — students who explore many combinations (pitch + rhythm, tempo + dynamics + silence, articulation + texture) build compositional thinking that serves them throughout the music curriculum.
success_criteria: Creates a composition or section that deliberately combines at least two named elements
Can describe the expressive effect they intended when combining those elements

nodes.label: Selecting elements for a purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can make deliberate decisions about which elements to use in a composition or performance to achieve a specific communicative or expressive intention.
nodes.minimum_width: Choose which elements to include in a composition or performance and state a reason connected to what they want the music to communicate.
nodes.typical_width: Make and justify element selections across multiple composition and performance contexts — e.g. deciding to use a slow tempo for a lullaby, choosing to use loud dynamics for an exciting section, selecting particular instruments based on their tone colour; practise a repertoire of songs using elements such as tempo, dynamics or articulation for expressive effect.
wider: Write lyrics for a chant/rap and select rhythmic patterns that match the mood or message of the lyrics — explain the connection
Use accessible technologies (recording device) to listen back to a composition and make decisions about which elements to change to better achieve the intended effect

response_modes.reason: Selection decisions require students to reason from intent to choice: 'What do you want this music to feel like? Which elements could help create that feeling?' Structured prompting — before composing — builds the habit of selecting with purpose rather than selecting by default.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Selection decisions are where musical thinking becomes compositional thinking. Students who practise selecting elements for different purposes (a lullaby vs an exciting piece vs a welcome song) develop transferable musical decision-making skills.
success_criteria: Selects at least two elements for a composition or performance and states a reason for each
Can explain how the selected elements serve the intended communicative or expressive purpose

nodes.label: Documenting and practising
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can notate or record a composition using signs, symbols or a recording device, and use this documentation to practise and refine the work.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one form of documentation (signs, symbols, drawing or recording) to capture a composition; use it during practice to maintain consistency.
nodes.typical_width: Use signs and symbols, graphic notation or available devices to document compositions; use recordings to listen back and make decisions about what to change; practise a repertoire of songs using documentation to support accuracy and refinement.
wider: Create a graphic score that represents a soundscape — use it as a performance guide and refine it based on what worked in rehearsal
Record a composition in progress, listen back, and make one documented change — compare the before and after recordings

response_modes.reason: Documentation enables practice — without it, compositions exist only in the moment and cannot be refined. The consolidation investment here is in making documentation habitual and functional: students should automatically reach for a recording device or notation tool as part of their composing process.

success_criteria: Documents a composition in at least one form (drawing, symbols, recording)
Uses the documentation during practice to maintain or refine the composition
